title: What is known about 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RE_1LE---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RE_1LE---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state machine halts from blank tape. It belongs to a family of six holdouts with almost the same table (F0 = 1LE, E1 = 0RE). Their tapes are made of the words 10 and 110, grouped in sections split by 000, and they grow slowly to the left. This page lists what has been established, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The engine is decoded and proved in Lean for every size and every layout. At an event the tape is a base-3 counter N, then a binary counter Z, then a chain of binary words; N and Z get 1 per event, and every word is a counter that, when it wraps, sends 3 to the next word (so a carry is multiplied by 3 at every separator, and an empty word passes 3 times what it got). This chain law covers every layout the run has shown (the plain cascade, the X layer and all later eras are special cases) and is proved in lean/Layers.lean for any number of words of any widths. Inside a layout the whole right side is one number that grows by 1 per event, so an era change happens only when a carry runs off the last word. Using this, a simulator that jumps from one era change to the next and runs each change cell by cell has followed the run through 74 changes of era, 5.1·1041 events (so at least that many steps), with no halt. What an era change hands on (the new widths and values, and how many base-3 digits it takes from N) is the open part; C never runs out of digits: instead the chain keeps gaining words.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 183 cells have been visited and 66 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Sweep rules
claims.text: The head crosses runs of the words 01, 10, 011 or 110 in one state, rewriting each copy the same way, for any number of copies and any surrounding tape.

claims.title: No halt in 3·10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator runs 3·10<sup>9</sup> steps without a halt.

claims.title: Where it can halt
claims.text: A closed tape language with windows of 6 cells (closed, found and checked by bbtools.ctl, not yet in Lean) allows a halt only with F reading a 1 and 110001, 110011 from the head on: the first 1 of a word 110 followed by a section break 000 1.

claims.title: The first section
claims.text: At its visits to the left end (in state E) the tape starts E>0 0 1 0 (1 1 0)^k …; the record values of k: 10 at step 6,741,512, 11 at step 41,755,007, 12 at step 523,217,185, 13 at step 1,019,661,408, 14 at step 1,421,446,771, 15 at step 2,626,803,218. Its left-end configurations coincide with those of 1RB---_1LC0RF_0RA0LD_1LE1LA_1RF0LF_0LC0RA at 47 of its first 50 visits (in the same order; that machine takes about 1.12 times fewer steps): the two machines do the same thing.

claims.title: Growth
claims.text: Each new 110 at the front costs about 2 to 3 times the steps of the previous one, the signature of a counter; the rest of the tape changes everywhere between visits, so the counter's digits are not simply blocks.

claims.title: The event rule, for every size
claims.text: From an event 0^∞ 1 0 [N] A> 0 [M] 1 [R] (N base 3 in 3-cell digits 100/110/010, M and R binary in 4-cell digits 0010/1010 and 1000/1010, low digit first) the machine reaches the next event with N + 1, M + 1 and, when M wraps, R + 3; 54 theorems, one per case (54 cases, exhaustive by construction of events.py, not by a Lean theorem; carries over k twos in N, i ones in M, j ones in R; the wrap of N at the left end), each with its exact step count and any tape beyond.

claims.title: The run follows the rule
claims.text: The run reaches the clean shape (R followed by 1 0 1 and blank tape) at step 132,141 (N = 35 (5 digits), M = 2 (2 digits), R = 0 (12 digits)); 5,556 (to step 3·106) consecutive events then follow the rule, until R = 4,095 = 212 − 1 at step 3·106, about to overflow. Counting all events of the form N, 0 [M] 1, anything: 42,230 of the first 3·106 steps follow from the previous one by the rule, 3,227 do not (wraps of M that reach the undecoded part).

claims.title: Token rows of the visit law
claims.text: Vis q x r x': the head enters the stream x from the left in state q and first leaves it to the left in state r, leaving x'. With tokens of two cells right of the event cell, 32 rows occur in 3·107 steps; each is a Lean theorem, conditional on the nested visits of the rest of the stream and valid for every stream.

claims.title: The a/z stream and M as a recursive visit law
claims.text: Everything from R on, blank tape included, is one stream of a = 10 and z = 00. A visit in state B turns the first z into a and every second a before it into z; it comes out in A when the first z is at an odd place (the binary increment of R, for every size: vb_odd, ve_odd) and in C when it is at an even place (vb_even). M + 1 without a wrap (m_inc) and with a wrap, where the stream gets three visits (m_wrap), for every size.

claims.title: The overflow of R is the even case of the stream law
claims.text: R has no end: when all its digits up to the blank tape are 1, the first z is at an even place and the visit comes out in C, leaving the digits shifted by one token. In the run of 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RA_0LB--- this first happens at step 20,645 (stream a18 then blank, left as (z a)9 a). That the event rule fails only there is read off the rules, not a Lean theorem.

claims.title: The cascade rule of the later layout, for every size
claims.text: From an event 0^∞ 1 0 [N] A> 0 [Z] 1 1 [C] 0 1 [R] (N base 3 as before; Z, the former M, in 4-cell digits 0010/1010; C binary in 4-cell digits 0001 = 0, 0101 = 1; R as before; lowest digit first) the machine reaches the next event with N + 1, Z + 1, C + 3 when Z wraps and R + 3 when C wraps; 162 theorems, one per case, each with its exact step count.

claims.title: The chain law, for every layout
claims.text: At an event the right side is 0∞ 1 0 [N] A> 0 [Z] 1 1 [W₁] 0 1 [U₁] 1 0 1 1 [W₂] 0 1 [U₂] … 1 0 1 1 [Wm] 0 1 [Um] 0∞: Z (digits 0010, 1010), each W (0001, 0101) and each U (1000, 1010) binary, lowest digit first, of any width, W and U possibly empty, any number m of pairs. From one event to the next: N + 1, Z + 1; when Z wraps, W₁ gets 3; each wrap of a W gives its U 3; each wrap of a U gives the next W 3, as long as no carry leaves the last word. Equivalently Z + 2|Z|/3 · (W₁ + 2|W₁|/3 · (U₁ + 2|U₁|/3 · (W₂ + …))) grows by exactly 1 per event. 23 visit rows (24 for E1 = 0RE) of blocks of 1, 2 and 4 cells, composed by induction over the digits of each word and over the list of pairs; the generator is this family's copy of the one first written for 1RB---_1LC0RF_0RA0LD_1LE1LA_1RF0LF_0LC0RA. The law holds whatever tape follows the last word (encT B): no visit reads past it unless a carry leaves it.

claims.title: The run follows the chain law
claims.text: In the first 50,000,000 steps, 699,724 pairs of consecutive full events in one layout follow the law (the number above gains exactly 1), with no mismatch; 6 pairs change the layout (changes of era), 4121 full events are in no layout.

claims.title: No halt through the first changes of era
claims.text: The simulator runs the machine cell by cell from blank tape; at each full event in a layout it computes from the chain law the last event before a carry would leave the last word, writes that tape and runs on cell by cell through the change of era. 74 changes of era, 5.1·10<sup>41</sup> events in all (each at least one step), 264,431 steps run cell by cell, no halt; at the end the chain has 13 words, 154 digits in all. Before each jump it checks the law on random events of the era, rebuilt and run cell by cell: 29,211 events, 0 mismatches. Rests on the chain law (Lean) and on the simulator's arithmetic (the number above, decoded back into words), which is not in Lean.

claims.title: No halt past the defects of the chain
claims.text: Later full events carry defects of the chain. With the chain law up to the first defect, the defect law below at each crossing, and the grammar prefix where neither applies, the run reaches about 10<sup>128</sup> events from blank tape with no halt; 505 self-checks against cell-by-cell runs found no mismatch. At about 10<sup>128</sup> events the event cell moves into the chain, so no full event comes; 6·10<sup>10</sup> more steps stay within the same 2,729 cells without a halt.

claims.title: What a change of era hands on
claims.text: At the end of an era the words are at or near their largest values; after the change they hold small values, the boundaries between words have moved by a digit, the last word has one digit more, and N has either gained 1 (the change is one event, and two words disappear) or lost 2 to 9 base-3 digits, depending on N mod 9 and more, which become new words. A rule for this hand-over, and whether a change of era can ever halt, are open.

claims.title: What a carry does at a defect
claims.text: A defect is one erased cell in a separator (after Z 11 read as 01, after a W 01 as 00, after a U 1011 as 1001). When a carry of c > 0 reaches it, the separator is restored and the carry goes on as c − 3. In 3·107 steps 535,801 consecutive pairs follow the law, 2 of them crossing a defect, 0 mismatches; 19 events not covered.

claims.title: The stage after 10<sup>128</sup> events
claims.text: At about 10128 events the head starts turning back at a cell 17 cells into the chain. Around that cell the tape is two chains: on the left, base-3 words of N parted by the cells 1010 (each one cell off from the next), where the lowest word gets 16 per pair of visits and a word that wraps sends 2 to the next; on the right, the chain of binary words, where the first word (one cell and U1) gets 2 and W2 gets 6 per pair, and a word that wraps sends 3. In 108 steps 226,899 consecutive pairs of visits follow this law with 0 mismatches. A simulator that jumps by it covers about 10127 more visits with no halt; 3,178 self-checks against cell-by-cell runs found no mismatch. Then a carry leaves the right chain and the turning cell moves 31 cells further in.

claims.title: The stages after it
claims.text: Each stage ends when a carry leaves the right chain, and the turning cell moves (mostly by 2 cells). Around the new cell the tape is the same two chains, with other gifts per visit. A simulator that fits those gifts on 40 cell-by-cell visits of each stage, checks them on every later cell-by-cell visit and jumps with them follows 400 stages from blank tape, about 10<sup>409</sup> visits (so at least that many steps), with no halt; 18,882 self-checks against cell-by-cell runs found no mismatch. The gifts are fitted here; the next two entries derive them.

claims.title: The stage law, for every layout
claims.text: The stages are events of the chain law with the word Z empty, and with a chain of base-3 words on the left (parted by 1010) in place of the single counter N. From one event to the next the left words get one increment, and a word that wraps sends 2 to the next, because a separator passes two increments on (five left rows, lv_d0 … lv_top). With Z empty, the right side gets one unit (Q + 3, a wrap sends 3 to the next word). The head passes the turning cell twice per event. So the fitted gifts of the stages are this law read two visits at a time. Proved for every Z, every list of left words and any tape after either chain.

claims.title: The run follows the stage law
claims.text: With the proved law ported in place of fitted gifts, the run from blank tape goes through 13 stages to about 10137 events (so at least that many steps), with no halt. 630 consecutive pairs of events run cell by cell follow the law and 5,172 spot-check events match it. There the tape after the chain holds an item 11 [Q] 11 [Q'] 01 [P], outside the grammar. Every carry out of the chain crosses it cell by cell, so the proved law no longer jumps far.

claims.title: Half-digit shifts
claims.text: The other kind of defect, a separator missing altogether or a separator after Z read as a, ad, zd or ac, makes the words after it be read again with W and U swapped when a carry meets it. Its law is not decoded. It stops the proved stage law at about 10137 events, at an item 11 [Q] 11 [Q'] 01 [P]. Also open: whether the stages go on forever.

claims.title: The layered shapes of the later run
claims.text: In the first 3·108 steps the full events have the plain layout only at steps 361,628 to 743,696 with C of 2 digits and R of 13 (7,284 events), and 7,283 consecutive pairs of them follow the cascade rule with no mismatch. The other full events carry more words between Z and R; their commonest shapes: Z1 d C5 a X2 d C12 (steps 1,345,591 to 3,700,299, 38,868 events); Z3 d C5 a X2 d C12 (steps 3,700,657 to 9,320,409, 155,476 events); Z2 d C2 a X6 d C2 R13 (steps 9,320,864 to 20,382,132, 207,300 events); Z1 d C3 a X1 d C7 a X2 d C12 (steps 20,382,881 to 43,294,701, 276,400 events); Z2 d c a d c a X4 d c a X8 d C2 R13 (steps 43,298,588 to 79,159,384, 40,948 events); Z2 d c a d c a X14 d C2 R13 (steps 79,162,340 to 299,999,424, 375,500 events).

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same tapes at another pace, whatever the states, as 1 other holdout (listed on the explainer page).

explainer.lede: Nobody knows whether it halts. Its engine is decoded and proved: a base-3 counter on the left and a chain of binary words on the right tick together, and each word that wraps sends 3 to the next. So between two changes of era the whole right side is one counter. A simulator built on this has followed the run for 5.1·10<sup>41</sup> events without a halt; what a change of era hands on is the open question.

Events of the run (74 eras followed), no halt.

The event rule (N+1, M+1, R+3 on a wrap) for every size, in Lean.

Consecutive events by the cascade rule in 3·10<sup>8</sup> steps, no mismatch.

sections.heading: Three counters on one tape
html: At the moments we call events (the head in state A, on a 0, just right of the left counter) the tape reads
0∞ 1 0 [N] A> 0 [M] 1 [R] …

• N, a base-3 counter: 3-cell digits 100 = 0, 110 = 1, 010 = 2, most significant first, its lowest digit next to the head;
  • M, a binary counter: 4-cell digits 0010 = 0, 1010 = 1, lowest digit first (next to the head);
  • R, a second binary counter after a single 1: 4-cell digits 1000 = 0, 1010 = 1, lowest digit first.
In the words a = 10, b = 110 of the older description, M's digits read as sections a| and aa, which is why the tape looked like sections of a's split by 000.

sections.heading: One event: N + 1, M + 1, and R + 3 when M wraps
html: From one event to the next the head runs right over M (and over R only when M wraps), comes back, crawls into N, adds one there and returns. The net effect:

counterchange per event
N+1 in base 3; trailing 2s carry; when N = 2…2 it becomes 0…0 with one digit more (the tape grows 3 cells at the left)
M+1 in binary; trailing 1s carry; from 1…1 it wraps to 0…0 (same width)
Runchanged, except when M wraps: then +3 in binary

So N counts events (mod 3width), M counts them mod 2width, and R gains 3 every 2width of M events: two different bases running side by side. Example from the run of 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RA_0LB--- (M with 2 digits, R with 8): at steps 12,203, 12,223, 12,243, 12,253, 12,345 the triple (N, M, R) is (5, 0, 92), (6, 1, 92), (7, 2, 92), (8, 3, 92), (9, 0, 95).

Each case of this rule is a theorem in lean/Events.lean, proved for every size: 9 cases for N (lowest digit 0 or 1 after 0, 1 or k+2 twos, or the wrap of 2…2 at the left end), times 6 for M and R (no wrap, carry over i+1 ones, or a wrap of M with i+1 digits combined with the 4 cases of R's two low bits and a carry over j ones). 54 cases (exhaustive by construction of events.py), one theorem each, with its exact step count, e.g. 12i + 12j + 10k + 116 steps for a carry over k twos in N, a wrap of M with i+1 digits and R ending in 10 followed by j ones. When M does not wrap, nothing right of M is read, so these rules hold whatever lies beyond.

sections.heading: How long the run keeps this shape
html: In the clean shape R is followed by 1 0 1 and blank tape. This run reaches it at step 132,141 (N = 35 (5 digits), M = 2 (2 digits), R = 0 (12 digits)) and then 5,556 (to step 3·106) consecutive events follow the rule, until R = 4,095 = 212 − 1 at step 3·106, about to overflow.

An overflow of R (its carry running into the cells after it) is not covered by the rules: there the head goes past R and rebuilds the right part; in 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RA_0LB--- the transition D1 (the only way into F, whose 1 halts) is used in the first 105 steps only at steps 138, 1,008, 3,177, 7,571 (before the clean shape) and 20,756, 53,353, 92,444, 92,861 (at the first three overflows of R). After the first overflows the cells right of R are no longer just 1 0 1: they hold a further structure starting 1 0 1 1 0 …, and M and R take other widths. Counting every event whose left part is N and whose right part starts 0 [M] 1, 42,230 events in the first 3·106 steps follow from the previous one by the rule and 3,227 do not (the wraps of M that touch the undecoded part); at step 3·106: N = 18,571 (9 digits), M with 1 digit, R with 5 digits.

sections.heading: Two words and a separator
html: Write a for 1 0 and b for 1 1 0. Apart from a few cells at the ends, the tape is a string of a's and b's broken into sections by extra 0s (0 0 0 between two 1s). At its visits to the left end the first section is a b b … b followed by a's and b's, and the later sections are mostly runs of a's. Writing 1 for a and 2 for b, the tape at step 645,244,842 of the first sibling is 1222222222222222 | 111 | 111 | 11111 | 111 | 12 | 11111112 | 111111111 | 11111 | 11111 | 1 | 111 | 1 | 11.

sections.heading: Sweeps and an inner counter
html: The head moves through runs of words in one state, rewriting each copy the same way, for example A turning 0 1 1 into 1 0 0 or B turning 1 0 into 0 1 (proved in Lean for any number of copies: a_right_01, a_right_011, b_right_10, b_right_11, b_right_110, e_right_10, e_right_11, e_right_110). Its excursions do not usually reach the ends: the turning points far from the left end follow the ruler pattern of a binary counter with digits four cells wide (in a stretch of 17,000 steps from step 28,601 of the first sibling the far turning points are 43, 47, 43, 51, 43, 47, 43, 55, … cells from the left end). The ends are visited rarely, and each visit to the left end finds the whole tape rearranged.

sections.heading: Six siblings
html: Five of the six differ only in E1 and F0 (F1 halts in all of them); F is entered only from D reading 1, so F0 runs every time D finds a 1, and the five really are different machines. The sixth is a relabelled relative. All six show the same tape language and the same slow front.

sections.heading: Where it could halt
html: The machine halts only when F reads a 1. A closed tape language with windows of six cells (an over-approximation of every configuration reachable from blank tape, found and checked by bbtools.ctl) allows that only with 110001, 110011 from the head on: F on the first 1 of a word 1 1 0 that ends a section. Whether the run ever puts F there is the open question.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.066). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.054).
After 109 steps the tape spans 183 cells (145 left of the start, 35 right), with a density of 1s of 0.361.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: A cascade, then layers of words
html:
After the first overflows of R a counter C appears between M and R. In its plain form an event reads

0∞ 1 0 [N] A> 0 [Z] 1 1 [C] 0 1 [R] 0∞

with N in base 3 as before, Z the counter called M above, a new binary counter C (4-cell digits 0001 = 0, 0101 = 1) and R as before. The rule becomes a cascade: every event adds 1 to N and to Z; when Z wraps, C gets 3; when C wraps, R gets 3. That is 162 cases, each a Lean theorem with its exact step count, and the same for all six siblings.

In this sibling the plain layout occurs only early in the run. The full events of the later run carry more words between Z and R (in tokens: Zk, Ck words of k digits, Xk a word of k a z/a a digits, Rk the last one):

sections.heading: One law for every era
html:
All the layouts of the run, the plain cascade, the X layer and everything after, are one shape: Z followed by a chain of binary words, alternately of two kinds (W with digits 0001, 0101 and U with digits 1000, 1010), separated by the blocks 1 1, 0 1 and 1 0 1 1, any of them possibly empty:

0∞ 1 0 [N] A> 0 [Z] 1 1 [W₁] 0 1 [U₁] 1 0 1 1 [W₂] 0 1 [U₂] … 1 0 1 1 [Wm] 0 1 [Um] 0∞

Every word is a binary counter, and every wrap sends 3 to the next word. Each event adds 1 to Z; when Z wraps, W₁ gets 3; when W₁ wraps, U₁ gets 3; and so on. An empty word wraps at once, so it passes 3 times what it got. In one number: Z + 2|Z|/3 · (W₁ + 2|W₁|/3 · (U₁ + …)) grows by exactly 1 per event. The rules of the earlier sections are special cases: the cascade is one pair (C, R), the X layer two pairs (∅, X) and (C, R), and for the X layer the law gives the odd-looking C + 24/2k (an empty W makes the 3 into 9, X of k digits takes 9 mod 2k and passes the rest on, times 3).

The law is proved in Lean for every number of words and every width (lean/Layers.lean), from 23 visit rows of blocks of 1, 2 and 4 cells composed by induction.

Because the right side is one counter, a simulator can jump straight to the last event before a carry would leave the last word, and run only the change of era cell by cell. The first eras of the run:

Through 74 changes of era, 5.1·1041 events, nothing halts. The chain keeps growing: at the end it has 13 words with 154 digits in all. Step through a layout below; the page can run the machine itself on the encoded tape to check that it leaves exactly the predicted words.

sections.heading: What is left
html: The engine is proved for every layout: N + 1 on the left, and on the right the chain law. A halt can only come during a change of era, when a carry runs off the last word: every event that follows the law is a run of the machine that never reads the halting 1. At the end of an era all words are near their largest values; after the change they hold small values, the boundaries between words have moved by a digit, the last word has a digit more, and N has either gained 1 or given 2 to 9 of its lowest base-3 digits to new words. Open: (1) a rule for this hand-over; (2) whether some change of era can ever put the head on the halting 1.

sections.heading: One visit of a stream
html: Cut the tape right of the event cell into tokens of two cells: z = 00, a = 10, c = 01. Everything from R on, the blank tape included, is one stream of a and z, and one visit of the head in state B does this to it: the first z becomes a, and every second a before it becomes z.

If the first z is at an odd place the visit comes out in state A: with digits a z = 0 and a a = 1 this is the binary increment of R. If it is at an even place (all digits 1 up to the blank tape) the visit comes out in state C and leaves the digits shifted by one token. So R has no overflow into something else; the rare case is a visit that comes out in C.

Both cases, and M's increment and wrap (three visits of the stream), are proved in Lean for every size from 32 token rows, each of which is a small theorem about one token and the nested visits of the rest. What the c tokens of M do after a visit that comes out in C is in those rows but not yet composed; that is where the question of halting now sits.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same tapes at another pace (observed, not proved). Leave the states aside and compare only the tape and the place of the head. Then a large part of the first 107 configurations of this machine are configurations of the machines below, in the same order and up to the end of the run. The steps at which they occur differ, the tables are not renamings of each other, and equal tapes with different states may be continued differently, so this does not tie the halting questions together.

  • 1RB---_1LC0RF_0RA0LD_1LE1LA_1RF0LF_0LC0RA: 8,928,153 configurations, the last at step 10,000,000 here and step 8,928,580 there

summary: Two-word sweeper: a base-3 counter N and a chain of binary words; each event adds 1 to N and to Z, and each wrap of a word sends 3 to the next (proved in Lean for every layout). The run has been followed through 74 changes of era (5.1·10^41 events) with no halt, and with the law on the grammar prefix past the defects of the chain (each erased cell takes one unit of carry) to about 10^128 events; there the event cell moves 17 cells into the chain, and two chain laws around the new cell (base-3 words on the left, each wrap sending 2) carry the run about 10^127 more steps, until the cell moves again; a simulator that fits each later stage's gifts and checks them follows 400 such stages, to about 10^409 steps, with no halt. Why the gifts take their forms is proved in Lean: the stages are events with Z empty and a chain of base-3 words on the left, and with that law the run is followed to about 10^137 events. The era changes and the half-digit shifts are open.
